vignette:
She sits in the chair across from me, back straight, hands resting flat on her thighs as though she's about to receive orders. Even in civilian clothes-a soft gray sweater, jeans-there's a readiness in her posture, a vigilance that never fully switches off. She is thirty-five, a police officer for twelve years, married to a man who works in IT. She tells me she came because her husband begged her, because she snapped at him last week when he touched her shoulder from behind while she was washing dishes. "I almost elbowed him in the face," she says, voice flat. "I saw his face and I didn't recognize him for a second. I saw someone else."

The someone else was about a year and a half ago. She was on patrol, solo, late shift. A call came in for a domestic disturbance at a rundown apartment complex on the edge of her district. She arrived before backup. The door was unlocked. Inside, a man-later identified as a known offender with prior assault charges-grabbed her by the vest, pulled her into the bedroom, and closed the door. She tells me she remembers the weight of her duty belt, the way it pressed into her hip as he forced her onto the mattress. She remembers the click of her radio hitting the floor. She remembers thinking, I am a police officer. I am trained for this. But her body did not obey. He held a knife to her throat and said he would kill her if she screamed. She did not scream.

The assault lasted maybe twenty minutes. She does not know exactly. She remembers the smell of stale cigarette smoke and the sound of a ceiling fan wobbling overhead. When it was over, he let her go. She called for backup, filed a report, went to the hospital. She cooperated with internal affairs. The man was arrested, convicted, sentenced to twelve years. She was told she did everything right.

But something shifted in the weeks that followed. She started checking her mirrors obsessively while driving. She began parking with her back to walls. She stopped eating lunch in the station break room because the door had no lock. She would step into closets at home to change clothes-anywhere without windows. Her husband noticed she flinched when he kissed her neck. She started working only day shifts, then requested desk duty. She told herself it was practical, not fear. "I'm still a cop," she says. "I just-I reassigned."

At night, she wakes at 2:17 a.m. almost every night-the time the call came in. Her heart pounds. Her palms sweat. She lies still, listening for footsteps, for a wobbling fan. Her husband sleeps beside her, and she feels a strange resentment toward his peace. She has not let him touch her intimately in nine months. She tells herself she's protecting him. "He doesn't deserve to be with someone who's broken," she says. Then she corrects herself: "I don't want to be touched."

She avoids crime scenes with male suspects. She avoids the hallway in the station that looks like the apartment hallway. She avoids watching movies with any kind of violence. She has stopped reading the news. She says the world feels smaller now, more dangerous. She checks the locks on her doors six times before bed. She replaced all the doorknobs in her house with keyed-entry locks. Her husband asked if she was preparing for a siege. She didn't laugh.

Her PCL-5 score is 65. She doesn't know that number, and I don't tell her. What I see is a woman who carries herself like a soldier in a war that has no front line. She tells me she used to love the unpredictability of patrol-the adrenaline, the feeling of being in control. Now she craves stillness. She keeps the blinds drawn. She deleted her police scanner app. She sits in her living room in the dark and tells herself she is safe. But her body does not believe her.
